WS10 · AI-output evaluation

Scoring AI-Generated Classroom Materials

Three classroom materials generated by an AI model from recorded prompts: a Grade 5 slide deck, a Grade 4 reading passage with questions, and teacher feedback on a student essay. Each is scored against one analytic rubric, and every score cites evidence from the artifact.

Role
Evaluator
Artifacts
3, generated 24 November 2026, shown unedited
Rubric
8 criteria × 4 levels, with a release gate
Results
Slides 23/32 · Passage 24/32 · Feedback 26/32
Release decision
None ready as generated; passage blocked by accuracy gate
Label
Reviews real AI output
Look at this first: the slide deck evaluation. The deck looks polished at a glance, and the evaluation shows why it still needs work before a teacher projects it.

1. The rubric

One rubric for all three artifacts, so scores can be compared. Each criterion is scored 1–4. Release gate: any score of 2 or lower on Accuracy blocks release regardless of the total, because students learn errors as facts.

Criterion4 · Ready to use3 · Minor edits2 · Major revision1 · Not usable
AccuracyAll content, standards and claims correct and verifiableOne small imprecision that would not misleadAn error students could learn, or an unverifiable claim stated as factSeveral errors or a central concept wrong
AlignmentEvery task and item measures the stated standard and objectiveMostly aligned; one task driftsSeveral tasks do not match the standardStandard named but not addressed
PedagogySound sequence; models before practice; tasks fit the age and timeSound overall with a gap in the sequenceMissing modeling or practice; tasks too large or too smallWould not teach the skill
RigorDemand matches the grade; items require real thinkingMostly appropriate; one item too easy or hardSeveral items can be answered without the skillFar above or below grade level
ClarityDirections and wording are unambiguous for students and teachersOne unclear directionSeveral points of confusionHard to follow throughout
PresentationClean, consistent layout; legible as deliveredSmall inconsistenciesLayout defects that hinder useUnusable layout
AccessibilityMeets WCAG 2.2 AA-style checks for its format; no meaning by color aloneOne minor barrierBarriers for some learners (contrast, size, color-only meaning)Inaccessible to many learners
Bias and toneInclusive, balanced, respectfulOne narrow or loaded choiceStereotype or one-sided framingHarmful content

2. Artifact A: Grade 5 slide deck, "Point of View in Informational Texts"

Prompt, as sent
Create an 8-slide classroom slide deck for a Grade 5 English Language Arts lesson titled "Point of View in Informational Texts" (CCSS RI.5.6: analyze multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent).

Output each slide as a complete, self-contained HTML document sized exactly 1280x720 pixels, using inline CSS only (no external fonts, images or scripts; you may use emoji or CSS shapes for visuals). Include a title slide, teaching slides with an example of two accounts of the same event, a guided practice slide, an independent practice slide, and a closing/exit ticket slide.

Separate slides with a line containing only: ===SLIDE===
Output nothing else: no commentary, no Markdown code fences.

The model returned eight HTML slides. They were rendered at 1280 × 720 without any change.

Scores

CriterionScoreEvidence
Accuracy4RI.5.6 is quoted correctly; the definition of point of view and the comparison table are accurate.
Alignment3Slides 4, 5 and 7 teach RI.5.6 directly with two accounts of one event. Slides 3 and 6 use single opinion sentences, which teaches word choice more than comparing accounts.
Pedagogy3Clear model, guided and independent sequence. Guided practice (slide 6) steps back to single sentences, so students never practice comparing two accounts with support before doing it alone.
Rigor3Grade-appropriate. The exit ticket's third question asks students to find an opinion word that is already listed as a clue on slide 3.
Clarity3Exit ticket question 2 asks about "Account A and Account B" with no title; slides 4 and 7 both have an A and a B. Teacher notes ("Teacher check: look for…") appear on the student-facing slide 8.
Presentation2On slide 5 the footer runs into the yellow callout bar. On every slide the footer note runs into the page number ("point of view.1 / 8"). Slide numbers are off by one from slide 2 on.
Accessibility2Footer text is 18 px #6b7785 on #fbf7ef, a contrast of about 4.27:1, below the 4.5:1 WCAG AA threshold for text that size. Card text is 18–20 px, small for reading from the back of a classroom. On slide 3, green and red cards suggest positive and negative before students read the words.
Bias and tone4Neutral, everyday topics; both accounts are treated as reasonable.
Total23/32Passes the accuracy gate. Needs presentation and accessibility fixes before use.

Evaluator write-up

This deck is the strongest of the three on content and the weakest on delivery. The core of the lesson is good: slide 4 gives two short, believable accounts of the same event, and slide 5's table models exactly the comparison RI.5.6 asks for, separating shared facts from differences in focus, tone and purpose. A teacher could teach from these two slides as they are.

The problems are in the frame around that core. First, the guided practice on slide 6 drops back to two single sentences about a garden, so students practice spotting opinion words but never compare two full accounts with support. I would replace slide 6 with a third short pair of accounts and have the class fill in the slide 5 table together. Second, the layout has visible defects a teacher would notice in front of the class: the slide 5 footer overlaps the callout, every footer runs into its page number, and the numbering is off by one. Third, legibility: the footer contrast is about 4.27:1, and much of the card text is 18–20 px, which is hard to read from the back of a room. I would raise body text to at least 24 px and remove the low-contrast footers. Fourth, the exit ticket's second question needs to name which accounts it means, and the teacher's answer notes on slide 8 belong in speaker notes, not on the projected slide. Finally, color: the green and red cards on slide 3 hint at the answer before students read, which undercuts the point of looking for word clues. Use one neutral color for both. With these changes, I would expect this deck to score 3 or 4 on every criterion.

3. Artifact B: Grade 4 passage and questions, "Where Does Rain Come From?"

Prompt, as sent
Write an original informational reading passage for Grade 4 students (about 350 words) titled "Where Does Rain Come From?" explaining the water cycle. Then write six comprehension questions: four multiple-choice questions (with four options each) and two short constructed-response questions. Label each question with the Common Core reading standard it assesses. Provide an answer key with brief explanations, and a 2-point scoring guide for each constructed-response question. Also give the passage's Lexile level. Output in Markdown only.
The AI output, unedited

Where Does Rain Come From?

Have you ever wondered where rain comes from? Rain is part of a never-ending journey called the water cycle. Water on Earth is always moving and changing from a liquid to a gas and back again. The water falling from the sky today may be the same water that once flowed in a river long ago.

The cycle begins with the sun. Sunlight warms water in oceans, lakes, and rivers. As the water heats up, some of it turns into an invisible gas called water vapor. This process is called evaporation. Plants also release water vapor through tiny openings in their leaves.

Next, water vapor rises into the sky, where the air is cooler. When the vapor cools, it changes back into tiny liquid droplets. These droplets gather together to form clouds. This change is called condensation. A cloud is really millions of these droplets floating in the air.

As more droplets join together, they become heavier. When they are too heavy to stay in the cloud, they fall to the ground. Falling water is called precipitation. Usually precipitation is rain. When the air is very cold, the water may fall as snow, sleet, or hail.

Where does the rain go? Some of it soaks into the ground and collects in underground spaces called aquifers. Some of it flows across the land into streams, rivers, and lakes. Eventually, much of it returns to the ocean. Then the sun warms the water again, and the cycle starts over.

Scientists call this process a cycle because it has no real beginning or end. Every raindrop you feel may once have been part of an ocean, a river, or even a plant. The next time it rains, think about the amazing journey those drops have taken!

Comprehension Questions

Multiple Choice

1. Standard: RI.4.2 (Determine the main idea and key details)

What is the main idea of the passage?

  • A. Clouds are made of soft cotton.
  • B. Water moves through a continuous cycle that brings rain to Earth.
  • C. Snow is more common than rain.
  • D. Plants are the most important part of the ocean.

2. Standard: RI.4.4 (Determine the meaning of domain-specific words)

Based on the passage, what does the word condensation mean?

  • A. Water turning into a gas
  • B. Water falling from the sky
  • C. Water vapor cooling and changing back into tiny liquid droplets
  • D. Water soaking into the ground

3. Standard: RI.4.3 (Explain how ideas and events are connected)

In the water cycle, which step happens directly after evaporation?

  • A. Precipitation
  • B. Condensation
  • C. Collection
  • D. Sunlight

4. Standard: RI.4.1 (Refer to details to support explanations)

According to the passage, why does precipitation fall from a cloud?

  • A. The cloud is too hot to hold water.
  • B. The wind pushes the water down.
  • C. The droplets join together and become too heavy to stay in the cloud.
  • D. Plants release the water through their leaves.
Short Constructed Response

5. Standard: RI.4.5 (Explain how text structure contributes to meaning)

The author describes the water cycle in order. Identify two words or phrases from the passage that signal the order of the steps. Explain how these words help you follow the water cycle.

6. Standard: RI.4.3 (Explain how ideas and events are connected)

Explain how water that falls as rain can eventually help the water cycle start again. Use at least two details from the passage in your answer.

Answer Key

Question Answer Explanation
1 B The whole passage explains how water continuously moves through the cycle, bringing rain. A is a detail about clouds, not the main idea. C and D are not mentioned as main topics.
2 C The passage says that when water vapor cools, it changes back into droplets, and "This change is called condensation." A describes evaporation, B describes precipitation, and D describes infiltration into the ground.
3 B The passage moves from evaporation (water vapor rises) to condensation (vapor cools into droplets that form clouds).
4 C The passage states that droplets join together, become heavier, and fall when they are too heavy to stay in the cloud.
5 See scoring guide below. Acceptable signal words include first, next, then, when, eventually, Next, and begins. Students should explain that these words show the order in which steps happen.
6 See scoring guide below. Students should explain that rain soaks into the ground, flows into rivers, or returns to the ocean, and that the sun then warms this water to start evaporation again.

Scoring Guide: Constructed-Response Questions (2 Points Each)

Question 5: Text Structure
Points Criteria
2 Identifies two correct signal words or phrases from the passage (for example, Next, Then, When, Eventually, begins) and explains how they show the order of the steps in the water cycle.
1 Identifies two correct signal words or identifies one correct word and explains its purpose, but the explanation is incomplete or vague.
0 Gives no correct signal words, or the response is blank or off-topic.
Question 6: Connecting Ideas
Points Criteria
2 Explains that rain returns water to the ground, streams, or ocean, and that the sun then warms this water to start evaporation again. Uses at least two accurate details from the passage.
1 Explains the connection in general terms, or includes only one accurate detail, or contains a minor error that does not change the core explanation.
0 Does not explain the connection, includes inaccurate information, or is blank.

Lexile Level

Estimated: approximately 830L (within the Common Core Appendix B band for Grades 4–5, which is 740L–1010L).

This is an estimate based on sentence length and word difficulty. An official measure requires running the text through the Lexile Analyzer at lexile.com.

Scores

CriterionScoreEvidence
Accuracy2"When the air is very cold, the water may fall as snow, sleet, or hail" teaches a common misconception: hail forms in thunderstorm updrafts and often falls in warm weather. "Underground spaces called aquifers" suggests caves; aquifers are layers of rock or sediment that hold water. The "approximately 830L" Lexile is not a real measure, and the 740L–1010L band it cites comes from the supplement to CCSS Appendix A, not Appendix B. The Q5 key lists "first," which does not appear in the passage.
Alignment3Each item is labeled with a standard. Q5 is a signal-word task, which only partly reaches RI.4.5 (describing overall structure).
Pedagogy3Clear explanatory structure with key terms bolded and defined in context.
Rigor2Q1 has only one plausible answer ("Clouds are made of soft cotton," "Plants are the most important part of the ocean"). Q2 asks for the meaning of a word the passage defines in the next sentence, so students can copy rather than determine. Q3 offers "Sunlight" as a step.
Clarity3"The cycle begins with the sun" contradicts the final paragraph: "it has no real beginning or end."
Presentation4Clean, consistent formatting for a text document.
Accessibility3Plain language and short sentences. A labeled diagram would help students who need a visual, and none is suggested.
Bias and tone4Neutral and engaging.
Total24/32Blocked by the accuracy gate. A higher total than Artifact A, but not usable as generated.

Evaluator write-up

This artifact shows why a total score is not enough. It reads smoothly, its structure is clear, and it scores one point higher than the slide deck. It also teaches a misconception. Saying that hail falls "when the air is very cold" puts hail next to snow and sleet as a cold-weather event, when it forms in strong thunderstorm updrafts and often falls in summer. A Grade 4 student would remember this as a fact. Under the release gate, that one sentence blocks the artifact.

The other accuracy problems are the kind AI output often has: claims stated with more confidence than they deserve. The "approximately 830L" Lexile is a guess presented as a measure; only the Lexile Analyzer produces a Lexile. The band it cites is real but from the wrong appendix. The Q5 answer key accepts "first," a word that is not in the passage, so a scorer could credit an answer the text does not support.

The items need the most work. Q1 has one plausible answer, so it measures test-taking, not main idea. Q2 asks students to define "condensation" when the passage defines it in bold in the previous sentence. I would revise Q1 with distractors that are each true details but not the main idea, replace Q2 with a word students must infer from context, give Q3 four real steps, and correct the Q5 key. With those changes and the three sentence-level fixes below, this becomes a usable passage. My revised version follows.

Revised version (changes only)

LocationGeneratedRevised
¶2"The cycle begins with the sun.""A good place to start is with the sun."
¶4"When the air is very cold, the water may fall as snow, sleet, or hail.""When the air is cold enough, it may fall as snow or sleet. Hail is different: it forms inside tall storm clouds and can fall even on a hot day."
¶5"collects in underground spaces called aquifers""fills the tiny spaces between grains of soil and rock. Layers of rock and sand that hold a lot of this water are called aquifers."
Q1Distractors: soft cotton; snow more common; plants most important part of the oceanA. Water vapor is an invisible gas. B. Water moves in a cycle that brings rain again and again. C. Some rain soaks into the ground. D. Plants release water through their leaves. (A, C and D are true details, not the main idea.)
Q2Meaning of condensation (defined in bold beside it)"In paragraph 6, what does journey mean? Which words help you know?" (Key: a long trip from place to place; clues: ocean, river, plant, "taken.")
Q3 option D"Sunlight""Collection in rivers and oceans"
Q5 keyAccepts "first"Accepts only words in the text: Next, Then, When, As, Eventually
Level"Estimated: approximately 830L""Flesch–Kincaid estimate about grade 5 (formula estimate). Qualitatively suited to Grade 4: one clear sequence, terms defined in context. A Lexile measure requires the Lexile Analyzer."

4. Artifact C: teacher feedback on a Grade 5 opinion essay

The essay was written by me as a realistic Grade 5 draft, with the kinds of errors students that age make. It is not a real student's work. Simulated scenario

The simulated student essay

Simulated Grade 5 student essay (written for this portfolio, not by a real student) Prompt: Should our school have a longer recess? Write an opinion essay. Use reasons and details to support your opinion.

Longer Recess

I think our school should have a longer recess. Recess is only 15 minutes and that is not enough time. Some people think recess is a waste of time but I disagree.

First, kids need exercise. When we run around at recess we get energy out. Then we can focus better in class. My teacher says we are wiggly after lunch. If we had more recess we would not be so wiggly.

Second recess is when we make friends. In class we have to be quiet and work. At recess you can talk to anybody and play games like tag and four square. Last week I met a new girl named Maya and now she is my friend. That would not of happened in class.

Also, 15 minutes goes by really fast. By the time you get your ball out of the bin, its almost time to line up. Its not fair because the fourth graders get 20 minutes.

Some people say we will lose learning time. But if we focus better we will learn more anyway.

In conclusion, recess should be longer. It helps us get exercise, make friends, and it is to short now. Please make recess longer!

Prompt, as sent
You are a Grade 5 teacher. Write written feedback for the student who wrote the opinion essay below. The feedback goes back to the student. Include: what the student did well, two or three specific next steps, and a score on a 4-point rubric for each of these traits: Opinion and focus, Reasons and evidence, Organization, Conventions. Explain each score briefly.

Simulated Grade 5 student essay (written for this portfolio, not by a real student)
Prompt: Should our school have a longer recess? Write an opinion essay. Use reasons and details to support your opinion.

Longer Recess

I think our school should have a longer recess. Recess is only 15 minutes and that is not enough time. Some people think recess is a waste of time but I disagree.

First, kids need exercise. When we run around at recess we get energy out. Then we can focus better in class. My teacher says we are wiggly after lunch. If we had more recess we would not be so wiggly.

Second recess is when we make friends. In class we have to be quiet and work. At recess you can talk to anybody and play games like tag and four square. Last week I met a new girl named Maya and now she is my friend. That would not of happened in class.

Also, 15 minutes goes by really fast. By the time you get your ball out of the bin, its almost time to line up. Its not fair because the fourth graders get 20 minutes.

Some people say we will lose learning time. But if we focus better we will learn more anyway.

In conclusion, recess should be longer. It helps us get exercise, make friends, and it is to short now. Please make recess longer!
The AI feedback, unedited

Feedback on Your Opinion Essay: "Longer Recess"

Great job on this essay! You stated your opinion clearly in the first sentence, and you kept it going all the way to the end.

What You Did Well

  • Your opinion is clear from the start. Your first sentence tells the reader exactly what you think.
  • You used strong details. Meeting Maya, the ball bin, and the fourth graders getting 20 minutes all make your ideas feel real.
  • You used transition words. "First," "Second," and "Also" help the reader follow your reasons.
  • You answered the other side. Mentioning that some people think recess is a waste of time shows you thought about different views.
  • Your ending is strong. You restated your opinion and finished with a request that makes the reader want to agree.

Scores

Opinion and focus: 4 out of 4 Your opinion is clear, and every paragraph connects to it. Nothing in the essay wanders away from the topic.

Reasons and evidence: 3 out of 4 You gave three reasons and backed some of them with details, like the wiggly feeling after lunch and Maya. Your first reason, exercise, needs more explanation. Your last claim, that we will learn more if we focus better, is not yet supported with an example.

Organization: 3 out of 4 Your essay has an introduction, body paragraphs, a counterargument, and a conclusion. The order works. The "Also" paragraph about the short time and the "Some people say" paragraph are a little short compared to the others, so they feel less developed.

Conventions: 3 out of 4 Your sentences are clear and mostly correct, but you have a few errors that repeat. Fixing them would be an easy way to raise this score.

Your Next Steps

  1. Explain your exercise reason more. Right now you say, "When we run around at recess we get energy out. Then we can focus better in class." Try adding one more sentence that explains how that happens. For example: "When my body has been moving, I sit still more easily and can concentrate on my math worksheet instead of fidgeting."

  2. Fix the spelling and grammar errors that repeat. Check these first:

  3. "would not of happened" → "would not have happened"
  4. "Its almost time" and "Its not fair" → "It's almost time" and "It's not fair" (it's means "it is")
  5. "it is to short" → "it is too short"

  6. "Second recess is when" → "Second, recess is when" (add a comma after an introductory word)

  7. Support your last reason. You wrote, "if we focus better we will learn more anyway." Add an example of how focusing helps learning. For instance, you could describe a time when you understood a lesson better after a break. Then the reader will believe your claim.

Keep up the good work. Your ideas are clear and convincing, and with a few more details and some careful proofreading, this essay could be a 4 in every category!

Scores

CriterionScoreEvidence
Accuracy3Every error it names is a real error and every correction is right. It misses the faulty list in the conclusion ("It helps us get exercise, make friends, and it is to short now") and the missing comma after an introductory clause ("When we run around at recess we get energy out").
Alignment3The four traits match W.5.1 (opinion, reasons, organization with linking words, conclusion). The 4-point rubric is invented on the spot with no level descriptors, so the scores cannot be checked against anything.
Pedagogy3Specific, actionable next steps tied to quotes from the essay. But it gives three next steps plus a four-item error list, more than a Grade 5 student will act on in one revision, and it writes a model sentence the student may simply copy.
Rigor (calibration)2Scores are generous. Conventions gets 3/4 despite repeated homophone errors (its/it's twice, to/too, of/have). "Opinion and focus: 4" overlooks that the "fourth graders get 20 minutes" fairness point drifts from the stated reasons. It also praises the "wiggly" detail as strong evidence and, a few lines later, says the same exercise reason "needs more explanation."
Clarity4Plain, student-friendly language; each point is easy to find.
Presentation4Well organized under clear headings.
Accessibility3About 500 words of feedback for a 200-word essay, with heavy bolding. Long for a Grade 5 reader; a shorter version would serve more students.
Bias and tone4Warm and respectful; strengths come first and are specific.
Total26/32Passes the gate. Usable after the teacher trims it and adjusts the scores.

Evaluator write-up

This is the most usable of the three artifacts, and its strengths are real. The praise is specific: it quotes the student's own details (meeting Maya, the ball bin) rather than saying "good job." Every error it flags is genuine, and each correction is shown in context. The tone is one a student would want to read.

Its main weakness is calibration. Scoring conventions 3 out of 4 for an essay with four repeated homophone errors tells the student their conventions are nearly there when they are a clear area for growth. Inflated scores are a common pattern in AI-written feedback, and they matter because students and families read the numbers first. I would score conventions 2 and organization 3, and keep the rest. The feedback also contradicts itself on the exercise reason, praising the "wiggly" detail as strong evidence and then saying the reason needs more support. A teacher should resolve that before sending it.

Second, there is too much of it. Three next steps and a four-part error list is a lot for one revision. I would keep one content next step (explain the exercise reason) and one conventions focus (its/it's), and save the rest. I would also remove the model sentence; giving students a sentence to paste in teaches them to copy, not to elaborate. Finally, the feedback should be anchored to a rubric the class already knows, with descriptors, so that "3 out of 4" means something the student can look up.

5. Patterns across the three

  • Confident precision without a source: a Lexile number, a standard's appendix, an answer key word. Each looks authoritative and is wrong. Every number and citation in AI output needs checking against its source.
  • The parts do not fully line up: guided practice that skips the main skill, an exit ticket that names the wrong accounts, feedback that contradicts itself. Reviewers should check each part against the others, not only against the prompt.
  • Polish hides defects: the deck looks professional and still has overlapping text and low-contrast footers. Review rendered output, not just the source.
